narrative.overview:
Game Traveler is a reference atlas for video games. The world is printed faintly on ivory with a smoke-blue sea, like a steamship chart, and everything a reader can act on is overprinted in two inks: deep midnight blue for structure and vermilion for destinations. The chrome is the atlas's furniture: a cream title bar with the wordmark and a live index line ("598 games / 685 places · 3100 BC–2310"), a sheet that docks to the left on desktop or rises as a bottom sheet on phones, and a list of every place by country for readers who would rather use the index than the map.

The type is one family, Archivo, in several widths. Titles and game names are condensed and heavy, release years are big tabular numerals in their own column, and controls and running text stay at normal width. The only other face is Newsreader italic, used for «Traveler» in the wordmark and for the line «A video game atlas»; everything else, including the welcome heading, is Archivo.

The audience is 30 to 60, so app text never drops below 13px (0.8125rem), touch targets are 44px, and every text pair passes WCAG AA. UI copy is English and speaks plainly: "Games in this area", not "cluster"; "The pin marks the area, not an exact spot", not "Representative map point".
keyCharacteristics: Faint, desaturated basemap; colour only where there is something to act on.
Vermilion (`magenta` token) is the one action, destination and route colour.
Midnight ink (`ink`) for text, rules, clusters and pressed controls.
Condensed heavy Archivo for titles, names and years; normal width for UI.
Square corners everywhere except things printed on the map.
The map shows games, not just numbers: clusters list their games on hover, and small clusters open as a list.

rules.name: The One Accent Rule
rules.body: Vermilion means "a place", "act here" or "this is the route". Never use it for genre or decoration.

rules.name: The Faint Map Rule
rules.body: Tiles are always desaturated (`grayscale(0.85) sepia(0.05) contrast(0.9) brightness(1.03)`, baked into the style in basemapTone.ts) so labels sit behind markers, not beside them; land is ivory (#f6f0e3) and the sea smoke blue (#b7cbd2), set after the tone. Rejected (3 November 2026): sepia 0.18 and contrast 0.78, which yellowed the whole map like newsprint, and a grey-beige sea barely darker than the land. Town and city names sit 1.2em off their point (variable anchor), so they never cover the place dot on it.

rules.name: The Ramp Rule
rules.body: Sizes come from 2.5 / 1.9 / 1.6 / 1.5 / 1.375 / 1 / 0.95 / 0.875 / 0.8125 rem, plus 1.25rem for the brand below 360px, 17/15px cluster numerals, 14px map text and 12px attribution.

rules.name: The Tabular Years Rule
rules.body: Every year, count and range uses tabular lining figures. Years before 0 read "N BC".

dos: **Do** keep the basemap faint and overprint only what can be acted on.

**Do** explain the rules to the reader: the More menu has "How places are chosen", a second tab of the info dialog, which restates in plain words what counts as a place, the three settings, dots versus sites versus country shapes, places within places, journeys, the link policy and My atlas. The About tab links to it.

**Do** give the browser's back button something to go back to: opening a place, game, country or search pushes a history entry (filters, route choice and map moves replace the address in place), and popstate rebuilds the panel, filters and map from the address exactly as a page load does. Rejected: replaceState for everything (the back button left the site after any number of taps).

**Do** draw the country shapes in the vector basemap (MapLibre, on the GPU), not as Leaflet SVG: Leaflet re-projected every polygon vertex on every zoom change, and that, not clustering, was most of what a zoom cost (333ms of a 4-zoom profile). The shapes are one GeoJSON source per scale keyed by ISO code; games, open, been and hover are feature state, so nothing is re-sent when the selection changes, and the layers sit under the basemap's labels. Hover and click come from the Leaflet map and are looked up with queryRenderedFeatures. The SVG layer remains only as the fallback when the vector basemap fails. The atlas tone of the basemap (grayscale 0.85, sepia 0.18, contrast 0.78, brightness 1.08) is baked into the style's colours at load (basemapTone.ts) instead of a CSS filter on the canvas: the filter desaturated everything drawn in the canvas, including the vermilion country shapes, and cost a full-canvas filter pass per frame. The same filter still applies to the raster tile fallback. The 1:50m borders are also simplified at build time to 0.02° (under a pixel at zoom 6.75, the last level before the shapes hide at 7; 100k vertices became 52k) and the 1:110m ones to 0.03°.

**Do** keep the catalogue in its own script chunk, parsed with JSON.parse (several times faster than object literals for a megabyte of records), preloaded next to the app; and ship the italic wordmark face as a 23KB instance (opsz 20, weight 450–500, basic Latin) instead of the 144KB variable file.

**Do** zoom a touchpad pinch fractionally around the cursor. A pinch arrives as ctrl+wheel events with small deltas; Leaflet's wheel handler batches them and rounds each batch up to a whole level, so a pinch on a Windows laptop hopped level by level. While the pinch lasts the layers are scaled with CSS, the way Leaflet's own finger pinch works (map._move with pinch), and the map lands on a zoom level with a single zoomend when it stops; setting the zoom per event cost 20 to 240 ms each, because every zoomend rebuilds clusters and labels. About one level per 40px of pinch. The desktop map snaps to quarter levels (phones to halves), so fits land closer to their places. Scroll-wheel notches still step about one level.

**Do** keep a second level of places, spots, inside cities: a site record (park, castle, square) whose parent is a city or neighbourhood, and only those: a church in Cornwall or a castle in Bavaria stands on its own, since a region is not a place you are "inside" the way you are inside Lisbon (with regions on the list, Barrow Hill's page grew an invented "Cornwall, England" row with the stone circle nested under it). The game rolls up to the city, which lists it with an "At …" row of chips naming the spots, and the spot itself appears on the map only from zoom 12 as an ink diamond with its name under it, so the world and country views stay as they are. Opening a spot zooms to at least 12. Opening any place zooms in until no other dot lies within the cluster radius of it (up to 14), so the pinned dot never sits on top of a cluster of the places it was just listed with (Rennes-les-Bains opened over a "2"). A city that has spots under it carries a small count in the corner of its dot below zoom 12, and opening it frames the city with its spots (up to zoom 14) and shows those spots at whatever zoom the frame lands on, so a dot never hides five places behind it (Rennes-le-Château looked like one place with five sites underneath). On the game page the list says where you are and where in it: the city is the row, and its spots sit indented under it with a diamond, each clickable; a journey stays a flat, numbered list. A game set wholly in one spot lists only the spot, so with the game open the map marks the park, not the park and the city on top of each other; the city row on the game page is synthesised from the catalogue. Rejected: spots as ordinary pins at every zoom (a dozen dots on top of Lisbon at the world view); spots only in the list (nothing to find on the map).

**Do** let the world scroll as far south as the phone sheet covers, so the strip above the sheet can show Antarctica and large countries; otherwise every southern fly gets panned back north and the country ends up under the sheet. A panel that is open in React but whose sheet is not yet in the DOM counts as a sheet at 62%, both for fits and for the world limit; otherwise the limit centres the world in the full map for a moment before the sheet arrives and the stops end up under it. The world limit is enforced in pixels on `moveend` (not with Leaflet's `maxBounds`: Mercator clamps latitude at 85°, so a limit below the world cannot be expressed as a LatLngBounds). Country shapes (the selected country, the been shading) are drawn only below zoom 7: closer in, the country is larger than the screen and its fill became a veil over the whole map (8 still felt late: at 7 a country already fills most of a phone screen). A country opened on a phone puts the sheet at its peek height (104px) and fits the country to the whole map above it with 16px margins; new content opened inside the country (a cluster list) lifts the sheet back to 62%. Rejected: fitting a country above a 62% sheet (the strip is about 180px on a phone: Norway was a speck at zoom 3 and the United Kingdom a 60px sliver under two clusters). Phones zoom in half steps down to 1 (desktop: whole steps from 2), because the strip is small: Russia fits at 1.5 and a route round the whole world (an F1 season) at 1; when the world is shorter than the map it is centred in the strip rather than pinned to the top. The minimum zoom never changes while the map lives: the cluster layer builds one grid per zoom level down to the map's minimum when it is added, and a minimum that moves afterwards either hides the pins that stand alone (Hawke's Bay vanished on desktop when the layer was built for 1 and the map's minimum was 2) or crashes when such a pin is removed (Murmansk, the other way round). Rejected: min zoom 1 only while a sheet is open, 2 otherwise. Fits for a sheet are always computed for the 62% sheet, whatever the sheet is doing: a sheet at peek goes back up when new content opens, and a sheet at 90% covers nearly the whole map, so a fit computed for it zoomed Norway out to the world. A cluster list is fitted with pin margins only (24px left, 32px top, 16px above the sheet, 72px right for the map buttons), not the 56/60px label margins that routes get: the strip above the sheet is about 180px on a phone, and with label margins the Oslo-area cluster stayed exactly as tight as it had been clustered. Every fit keeps at least 80px of height even when the sheet covers more, so it never collapses to the minimum zoom. The panel's sequence number only ever grows, also after the panel has been closed: the country layer remembers the sequence it last fitted, and when the count restarted at 1 after a close, the next country tapped got the same number and was never fitted (zoom in a little, tap Brazil, and only its top showed above the sheet). A point that is a whole country opens the country even when a fictionalised area record shares its coordinates (Greece, India); country records sit on the country's label point, not on a city (Germany's sat on Trier, Turkey's on Marmaris, Kenya's on the Safari Rally). The fit covers the country's main part (the polygon holding its label point), the other parts within 8° of the label (archipelagos: the Bahamas, Palau, both islands of New Zealand, Crete, Corsica) and its places with games within 12° of the label: Norway's mainland without Svalbard (16° north of the label) or Jan Mayen (18° west; it cost a zoom level on phones and showed mostly sea, and it stays in the panel), Greece with Crete, France without French Guiana, the USA without Hawaii, Easter Island left to the panel. Rejected: all parts within 35° (Svalbard forced Norway to zoom out to the whole North Atlantic); the main part alone (the Bahamas, Palau and Kiribati were framed on one island with the rest of the chain off screen, and New Zealand on the South Island only).

**Do** let the map go round the world: panning east past Japan arrives in the Americas (`worldCopyJump`), and markers, routes and pins repeat on each copy. Only latitude is bounded, so there is no grey void above the Arctic or below Antarctica. Rejected: a longitude limit at ±180° (it stopped the map at the date line).
**Do** show games, not just counts, as early as possible.
**Do** keep every overlay docked to an edge and never stack two over each other.
**Do** offer a non-map path (search, place index) to everything on the map.
**Do** set titles and years in condensed Archivo, and controls and text at normal width.
donts: **Don't** use Newsreader outside the wordmark and tagline, or fall back to a system serif.
**Don't** use uppercase for headings; only genre tags are uppercase.
**Don't** put shadows on docked panels, or use heavy shadows anywhere; only floating elements get the one soft shadow.
**Don't** show raw coordinates or cartographer jargon to readers.

**Don't** add a game just because a real place is in its title or on its box. The place has to be depicted: a recognisable street, landscape or landmark the player moves through. Chicago 90 (a grid labelled Chicago) and Test Drive II's scenery disks (generic roads labelled with six countries) were added on 30 October 2026 and taken out the same day; Test Drive III stays because its Northern California run from the coast to Yosemite is drawn as that landscape.

**Don't** open a location note by restating where it is ("The Italian stop", "The Swiss stop", "The Greek level"): the reader is looking at Venice, so the note starts with what happens there. Don't cite the source in the note either ("named by the publisher", "the source identifies"); the note says what happens, the source field says where we got it.

**Don't** explain pin placement in a location note when the place is real ("the pin marks the country", "representative anchor"): the quiet line under the place already says "pin marks the area", and the note says what happens there. When the pin is an interpretation, that is, the place is invented and we chose where to put it, the note may say why in a few words ("pinned on Duloe stone circle, which the designer walked"), and the fictional place's own record always does. Refined 30 October 2026: the explanation is allowed for invented places, never required, and never for real ones.
**Don't** place ads before the reader has seen any games.
**Don't** fabricate imagery; IGDB covers are the only pictures.
